# Considerations in High Dimensions Activity
The purpose of this Quarto document is to explore how AI (when prompted carefully and appropriately) may provide understandings of complex topics; albeit, provided explanations should be interpreted with caution.

## Concept Clarification
One concept I found particularly difficult to grasp was multicollinearity in a high dimensionality space. While the textbook explains briefly the issue with mutiple correlations among predictors and their associated response, I found the explanation and included example to be full of jargon. Knowing this concept is important for interpretations in high-dimensionality settings. As such, I chose this specific concept for further clarification. 

## Prompt 
I prompted Claude to provide a clear breakdown of this concept. Below are the list of prompts I asked it to explain to me so I could better understand high-dimensional multicollinearity. 

1. "I am an environmental data science student who knows data science concepts and applications. While reading Chapter 6.4 of my machine learning textbook titled 'An Introduction to Statistical Learning with applications in Python', I came across the dangers of multicollinearity in a high-dimensional setting. However, I am struggling to imagine and visualize what this signifies. Please give me a simplified example of what exactly multicollinearity in a high-dimension setting looks like and why it is critical to understand regarding interpretation." 

2. "Please simplify your explanation of the diagram you provided as well as excluding any mathematical notation."

-**Answer**: "Here's the simpler version.
Multicollinearity means some of your predictors are basically telling you the same thing. In a watershed, "% cropland" and "fertilizer use" rise and fall together — so they're near-duplicates.
When you have just two duplicate predictors, your model can't tell their effects apart. It can credit one or the other (or split it any way) and the predictions come out the same. So the coefficients become unstable and untrustworthy.
In a high-dimensional setting you don't have two duplicates — you have dozens of predictors that all move together, and very few observations. Now the problem explodes: many different combinations of predictors fit the data equally well. That's exactly what the diagram shows. Three models, almost no predictors in common, all with the same R². The data simply cannot tell you which set is the "right" one.
Why this matters for interpretation: if your model selects "septic density" as important, you cannot conclude septic systems cause algae. A different equally-good model blamed cropland instead. The real driver might be phosphorus — something you never even measured — and all your predictors are just stand-ins for it.
So the one thing to remember: in high dimensions with correlated predictors, you can still build a model that predicts well, but you cannot trust it to tell you which variables actually matter. Prediction is fine; explanation is not."


## Reflection
I opted to use Claude to clarify this topic in the simplest terms possible. My first prompt produced a very insightful diagram of an example with many aquatic variables that were severely correlated and how cross validation was used on three models to compared the "best" R squared value, concluding that all three simulated models predict lake algae very well but each had different *drivers*; the data can't conclude which predictors are causal across all three models. While the diagram was very insighful, the accompanying explanation was an eyesore; in my opinion, it was worse than the explanation provided in the book! Ultimately, it took two iterations to return a simplified but meaningful explanation of exactly why multicollinearity matters for careful interpretation in a high-dimensional space: you cannot just conclude that a predictor like "septic density" is important for predicting lake algae because there could be another "good" model that identified cropland as the main driver instead. When I cross-compared Claude's answer with the book, I found that both explanations matched; the SNP example in the textbook is more clear. I now understand that one should not generalize results because there could be many models affecting the outcome and should be further validated on different datasets.
